name: Stomach
func: A stretchy muscular bag that stores food, churns it with acid and enzymes into a soupy mix called chyme, and releases it slowly into the small intestine. Its acid also kills many germs.

levels.kid:
Your **stomach** is a stretchy bag shaped a bit like the letter J. It's on the upper left side of your tummy, just under your ribs.

When you eat, food comes down the food pipe and lands in your stomach. The stomach can stretch to hold a big meal, a bit like a balloon.

Then it gets to work! Its walls squeeze and churn to mash the food, and it adds super-strong **acid** and special helpers called **enzymes** that start breaking down foods like meat and cheese. The acid also kills lots of germs that came in with your food.

After a few hours, the food has turned into a thick soup. The stomach lets it out a little at a time into the small intestine.

When your stomach is empty, it sometimes makes a growling sound!
levels.hs:
The **stomach** is the widest part of the gut, lying mostly in the **left upper quadrant** and **epigastrium**, under the left dome of the **diaphragm**. In front of it are the left lobe of the **liver** and the anterior abdominal wall. Behind it, separated by a space called the **lesser sac**, lie the **pancreas**, left kidney and adrenal, and the **spleen** sits to its left and behind.

It has parts:
- **Cardia**: where the esophagus joins (at about T11).
- **Fundus**: the dome bulging up above the cardia, often holding a gas bubble.
- **Body**: the large central part.
- **Pylorus**: the funnel-shaped exit, made of the **pyloric antrum**, pyloric canal and the thick **pyloric sphincter**, which leads to the **duodenum** (at about L1, the **transpyloric plane**).

It has a short concave **lesser curvature** (right side) and a long convex **greater curvature** (left side). When empty, the inner lining forms folds called **rugae**, which flatten out as it fills; it can hold over 1.5 litres.

Main jobs: **storing** food, **mixing** it into **chyme**, starting **protein digestion** with acid and **pepsin**, killing microbes, and making **intrinsic factor**, which the body needs to absorb **vitamin B12** further down the gut.
levels.college:
**Gastric glands** contain several cell types:
- **Parietal (oxyntic) cells**, in the body and fundus: secrete **hydrochloric acid** and **intrinsic factor**.
- **Chief cells**: secrete **pepsinogen** (activated to pepsin by acid) and gastric lipase.
- **Mucous neck cells** and surface mucous cells: mucus and **bicarbonate**, forming a protective gel layer.
- **Enteroendocrine cells**: **G cells** (in the antrum) make **gastrin**; **D cells** make **somatostatin**; **ECL cells** release **histamine**.

The muscularis externa has three layers: **inner oblique**, middle circular and outer longitudinal, which allows powerful churning.

**Blood supply** comes from all three branches of the **coeliac trunk**: the **left gastric** and **right gastric arteries** run along the lesser curvature; the **right and left gastroepiploic (gastro-omental)** arteries run along the greater curvature; and **short gastric arteries** from the splenic artery supply the fundus. This rich supply means the stomach rarely suffers ischaemia.

**Peritoneum**: the **lesser omentum** connects the lesser curvature to the liver; the **greater omentum** hangs like an apron from the greater curvature, covering the intestines.

**Nerves**: the **anterior and posterior vagal trunks** carry parasympathetic fibres that increase acid secretion and movement; sympathetic fibres come from the **coeliac plexus** (T6–T9), which also carries pain fibres, explaining why stomach pain is felt in the **epigastrium**.

**Phases of acid secretion**: **cephalic** (sight, smell, thought of food, via the vagus), **gastric** (stretch and protein in the stomach, via gastrin) and **intestinal** (mostly inhibitory feedback from the duodenum).
levels.phd:
**Acid secretion** at the parietal cell: the apical **H+/K+-ATPase (proton pump)** exchanges hydrogen ions for potassium, concentrating acid about a million-fold (gastric pH can fall to about 1–2). Carbonic anhydrase generates H+ and bicarbonate inside the cell; bicarbonate leaves basolaterally in exchange for chloride (producing the "**alkaline tide**" in the blood after meals), and chloride exits apically through channels. When stimulated, **tubulovesicles** carrying the pumps fuse with the membrane to form deep **secretory canaliculi**.

Three stimulants act synergistically: **acetylcholine** (M3, via calcium), **gastrin** (CCK2 receptors, via calcium, mainly acting indirectly by making ECL cells release histamine) and **histamine** (**H2 receptors**, via cAMP), which is why H2 blockers and proton pump inhibitors are both effective. **Somatostatin** from D cells is the main brake, released when antral pH falls.

**Motility**: the fundus and proximal body show **receptive relaxation** and **accommodation** (vagal, nitrergic), so pressure barely rises as the stomach fills. The distal stomach mixes with peristaltic waves at about **3 per minute**, paced by the **interstitial cells of Cajal**, a pacemaker network in the greater curvature. The antrum grinds food against a closed pylorus (**retropulsion**) until particles are under about 1–2 mm. Between meals the **migrating motor complex**, driven partly by **motilin**, sweeps leftovers onward.

The gastric mucosa's defence includes the mucus-bicarbonate layer, tight junctions, rapid cell renewal and **prostaglandins**, which boost mucus and blood flow.

***Helicobacter pylori*** survives acid using **urease** (making ammonia), flagella and adhesins. Strains carrying **CagA**, injected via a type IV secretion system, raise cancer risk. Its discovery (Marshall and Warren, Nobel Prize 2005) overturned the idea that stress alone caused ulcers; Marshall famously infected himself to prove it.

Stomach also makes **ghrelin**, the "hunger hormone", from X/A-like cells in the fundus.
levels.expert:
**Exam and history**: epigastric pain, **dyspepsia**, early fullness, nausea, vomiting. Red flags warranting urgent endoscopy include **unintentional weight loss**, difficulty swallowing, persistent vomiting, a mass, and signs of bleeding: **haematemesis** (vomiting blood or "coffee grounds") or **melaena** (black tarry stools).

**Peptic ulcer disease**: the main causes are ***H. pylori*** and **NSAIDs**. **Duodenal** ulcers are more common than gastric ulcers. A **posterior duodenal ulcer** can erode the **gastroduodenal artery** and bleed heavily. **Perforation** causes sudden severe pain, a rigid abdomen and free air under the diaphragm on an erect chest X-ray. Tests: **urea breath test** or stool antigen for H. pylori; endoscopy with biopsy. Treatment in general terms: acid suppression and H. pylori eradication; endoscopic control of bleeding; surgery for perforation.

**Upper GI bleeding** is risk-scored (e.g. **Glasgow-Blatchford score**) and managed with resuscitation and early endoscopy.

**Gastric cancer**: mostly **adenocarcinoma**, linked to H. pylori. Signs of spread include a hard node above the left clavicle (**Virchow's node**, **Troisier's sign**), a periumbilical nodule (**Sister Mary Joseph nodule**), and spread through the peritoneum causes ascites. **Linitis plastica** is a diffuse type that makes the stomach rigid like a leather bottle.

**Gastric outlet obstruction** (from scarring or cancer, or **pyloric stenosis** in babies with projectile vomiting and an "olive" mass) causes vomiting and a **succussion splash**.

**Neuro relevance**: **Cushing ulcers** are stress ulcers seen after severe brain injury or raised intracranial pressure, thought to result from vagal overactivity and acid hypersecretion; neurosurgical ICU patients often get **stress-ulcer prophylaxis**. **Pernicious anaemia** (autoimmune destruction of parietal cells, losing intrinsic factor) causes **vitamin B12 deficiency**, which can lead to **subacute combined degeneration** of the spinal cord.

**Surgery**: partial or total **gastrectomy**; bariatric operations (sleeve gastrectomy, gastric bypass).

keyPoints: J-shaped bag in the left upper quadrant under the diaphragm
Parietal cells make HCl and intrinsic factor; chief cells make pepsinogen
H. pylori and NSAIDs are the main causes of ulcers
Loss of intrinsic factor → B12 deficiency → spinal cord damage

test.explain: Parietal (oxyntic) cells use the H+/K+-ATPase to secrete acid, and also make intrinsic factor.

test.q: The enzyme that bacteria like H. pylori use to make ammonia is ______.
test.explain: Urease splits urea into ammonia, buffering acid around the bacterium; the urea breath test detects it.

test.q: Which artery supplies the stomach's fundus via short branches?
test.explain: Short gastric arteries from the splenic artery supply the fundus.

test.q: Stress ulcers after severe brain injury are called:
test.explain: Cushing ulcers follow brain injury or raised intracranial pressure; Curling ulcers follow severe burns.

test.q: The 'hunger hormone' made by the stomach is ______.
test.explain: Ghrelin rises before meals and stimulates appetite and growth hormone release.

test.q: What does the stomach make that's needed to absorb vitamin B12?
test.explain: Intrinsic factor binds B12 so it can be absorbed in the terminal ileum.
